## How people watch {#how}

The same story as the structured doc, but every exhibit removed and lists folded into paragraphs so the argument lives only in prose. That should trip the wall-of-text checks.

Most sessions are under a minute. People open Reels first about forty-one percent of the time, then Stories near twenty-eight, then the feed for the rest. Night peaks matter: publishing near two in the morning or a few seconds before the hour is how teams A/B test timing. Formats, timing and creative all interact, so a reader without tables or charts has to hold every number in their head while scrolling a long page of text. Teams repeat the same story in one paragraph instead of splitting it, which is deliberate: the paragraph should cross the long-paragraph threshold so D4 fires while the section still has no exhibit. The sentence keeps going with more detail about cohorts, holdouts, creative swaps, regional cuts, device mix, notification hooks, and editorial calendars so word count climbs without adding structure. Product wants a visible failure, not a subtle one, so this block keeps stacking clauses until a reader would rather skim a table that is not there.

## When they scroll {#when}

Another long section with no figure between headings. Teams track hour-by-hour opens, compare twelve against eighteen and twenty-two hundred, and still write paragraphs because nothing breaks the run. The prose share should dominate the word count while exhibits stay at zero, which is exactly the failure mode product cares about.

Peak hours, creative swaps, and holdout groups all get explained in sentences instead of exhibits. Readers deserve structure; this fixture deliberately withholds it.

## Takeaways {#out}

Lead with Reels, keep Stories tight, post near two in the morning, test five-second offsets before the hour, and repeat the same guidance in a third section that again has no table or chart. More words here push the section over the bare threshold so D6 can fire on headings that never gained an exhibit.
